title: Food and ordering at a warung
goal: Order food and drink from start to payment, choose how spicy you want it, and understand what the seller asks you.
bekal: order with *pesen* / *mesen* and say how many
close the deal: ask for the bill, pay, say thank you

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Ing warungé Bu Sri
dialogs.intro: Dian and Rini finally reach the warung (a small family-run eatery). Bu Sri is much older, so both use krama; Bu Sri answers in a mix of krama and ngoko, like most real sellers.

lines.speaker: Bu Sri:
lines.id: Come in, miss. What would you like to eat?

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.id: Do you have fried rice, ma'am?

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Sekedhik mawon, Bu. Kula boten kiyat pedhes.
lines.id: Just a little, ma'am. I can't handle spicy food.
lines.literal: a-little just, Ma'am. I not strong spicy.

lines.speaker: Rini:
lines.text: Kula pecel mawon, Bu. Sambelipun kathah.
lines.id: I'll just have pecel, ma'am. Lots of chili sauce.
lines.literal: I pecel just, Ma'am. chili-sauce-its much.

lines.speaker: Bu Sri:
lines.text: Ngunjuk napa? Ès tèh napa tèh anget?
lines.id: Anything to drink? Iced tea or hot tea?
lines.literal: drink what? ice tea or tea warm?

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Ès tèh kalih, Bu. Sing boten kathah gendhisipun.
lines.id: Two iced teas, ma'am. Not too sweet.
lines.literal: ice tea two, Ma'am. that not much sugar-its.

lines.speaker: Bu Sri:
lines.id: Right. Just a moment — it's still frying.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.id: Ma'am, how much is it altogether?

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Menika. Matur nuwun, Bu. Éca sanget.
lines.id: Here you are. Thank you, ma'am. It was delicious.

notes: **Badhé dhahar punapa?** — Bu Sri uses *dhahar* (krama inggil) for her customer's action, and Dian talks about herself without *dhahar*. The pattern from Unit 9 repeats here, and it will repeat every day.

**Napa** is the madya (middle-level) form of *punapa*, and at a warung you'll hear it far more than the full form. *Pedhes napa boten?* = spicy or not? Here *napa* means "or" — a job you already saw *apa* do in Unit 3.
**Kiyat** (krama) / **kuwat** (ngoko) means "strong". *Boten kiyat pedhes* (I can't handle spicy) is the standard way to refuse chili — gentler than saying you don't like it.

**Dipun-goréng** is the krama passive: the prefix *di-* becomes *dipun-* in krama. The ngoko form is *digoréng*. Passives are covered fully in Unit 18; for now just recognize *dipun-* before a verb as "being …-ed".
**Kesesa** means "in a hurry". *Boten kesesa* (no hurry) is a polite, very useful line when a seller apologizes for the wait — it eases things at once.
**Éca** is the krama of *énak* (tasty). Praising the food after you eat isn't just politeness in Java; it's part of the transaction, and the seller remembers it.
**Sedanten** is another form of *sedaya* (all), common in Yogyakarta. Both are correct.

grammars.title: Ordering: a pattern that always works
body: One pattern works at almost every warung in Java, and it has three parts: **dish + number + softener**.
after: **The number follows the item**, not the other way round: *sega goréng siji* ("fried rice one"), not *siji sega goréng* — the opposite of English.
**Nganggo** means "to use, with" and covers anything added: *nganggo sambel* (with chili sauce), *nganggo endhog* (with egg), *nganggo gula* (with sugar). Krama *ngangge*.
If you get really stuck, **pointing and saying *menika setunggal, Bu*** ("one of these, ma'am") will settle any order in Java. Nothing wrong with that.

blocks.text: **Wédang** has no exact English match: it means any **hot** drink. *Wédang jahé* (ginger), *wédang uwuh*, *wédang tèh*. In Yogyakarta, the roadside night stalls that sell wédang are called **angkringan**, and their tiny rice packets are **sega kucing** — "cat rice", because the portion is about the size of a cat's dinner.
**Legi** (sweet) is also the name of one of the market days from Unit 6 — exactly the same word. Javanese is full of double-duty words like this, and context always separates them.

sections.title: Being offered food: what's really going on

blocks.text: If you visit someone in Java, you'll be served something. If you walk past people eating, you'll be invited to join. It isn't empty talk, but it isn't an invitation you must accept either. There's an etiquette, and it's quite simple.

blocks.title: Three unwritten rules
items: **Touch what you're served**, even if it's just a sip. Refusing outright reads as keeping your distance. If you truly can't, give a reason: *nuwun sèwu, kula sawek boten sakéca* (sorry, I'm not feeling well).
**An invitation from someone already eating at a warung** is almost always just politeness. The right reply is *matur nuwun, sampun* (thank you, I've eaten), not sitting down with them.
**Wait to be invited before you start.** The key word is *mangga*. Until the host says it, the food on the table is just for looking at.
Ès tèh ____ boten kathah gendhisipun. (that, which)
